(COX2) activity, leading to decreased prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) production. Likewise, in a mouse model for Parkinson’s disease,
gT prevented damage to dopaminergic neurons by treatment with 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) better
when compared to aT. When vascular and lymphatic endothelial cells were exposed to physiological levels of aT, gT, or dT (0–
40 mM), no toxicity was observed but dT was more potent to limit cell behaviors related to inﬂammation/angiogenesis.
Intestinal epithelial cells may be more exposed to the different vitamin E analogs present in the diet. In adult and fetal-derived
intestinal epithelial cell lines, the peroxyl radical-induced membrane oxidation and inﬂammatory response were prevented by the
vitamin E analogs in the order dT > gT > aT. Interestingly, at concentrations of 50–100 mM apoptosis-induced cytotoxicity was
increased by dT and gT, whereas aT was not cytotoxic. These results point out an important role of the non-essential dietary vitamin
E analogs during their absorption by the intestine, at least until they become metabolized and eliminated by the liver.
